procedural_history.originating_court: Assistant Sessions Judge at Purnea in the State of Bihar
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment dated September 17, 1974 passed in Criminal Appeal No. 579 of 1969 by the Patna High Court, which confirmed the conviction and sentence imposed by the trial court.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The High Court of Patna dismissed Criminal Appeal No. 579 of 1969, thereby confirming the trial court's conviction of the appellant under section 376 of the Indian Penal Code and the sentence of five years rigorous imprisonment.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant filed an appeal by special leave against the High Court's judgment. The Supreme Court, after considering the evidence and submissions, dismissed the appeal and directed the appellant to surrender and undergo the remaining part of the sentence.

directions: The appellant who is on bail is directed to surrender.
The appellant is directed to undergo the remaning part of the sentence imposed on him.

issue.issue_text: Whether the approach adopted by the High Court and the trial court to the case is correct and whether the material is sufficient to warrant the conviction recorded by them.

facts: The appellant was convicted of rape by a trial court and the conviction was upheld by the High Court.
The conviction was based on the evidence of the victim (prosecutrix) and other prosecution witnesses examined at the trial.
During the appeal, the Supreme Court ordered the examination of two additional witnesses who had been mentioned in the original complaint.
These two additional witnesses did not support the prosecution's case and were considered hostile.
law: The fact that some witnesses turn hostile does not, by itself, prevent a court from finding an accused guilty.
A conviction can be sustained if there is other acceptable and credible evidence to support the prosecution's case.
application: The Supreme Court noted that while the two newly examined witnesses turned hostile, this was not determinative of the case's outcome.

The Court gave weight to the fact that both the trial court and the High Court had found the evidence of the victim and the other original prosecution witnesses to be believable and sufficient for a conviction.
The Court decided that the credible evidence from the original trial was enough to uphold the conviction, despite the hostile testimony of the new witnesses.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the judgments of the lower courts were correct and did not require interference. It found that there was sufficient acceptable evidence to warrant the conviction, and therefore, it dismissed the appeal and confirmed the appellant's conviction and sentence.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the approach adopted by the High Court and the trial court to the case is correct and whether the material is sufficient to warrant the conviction recorded by them.
appellant_arguments: The evidence was insufficient for a conviction, as key witnesses mentioned in the original complaint, including the local Mukhiya, did not support the prosecution's case when they were later examined.
respondent_arguments: The conviction was warranted based on sufficient evidence. The complainant's testimony had a 'ring of truth' and was corroborated in material particulars by other witnesses. Specifically, Sheikh Lafid (P.W. 1) saw the appellant on top of the complainant, Juman Nadaf (P.W. 2) saw the appellant fleeing the scene, and the complainant's husband, Jitrai (P.W. 4), testified that she reported the incident to him shortly after it occurred, which has corroborative value.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A conviction based on the uncorroborated evidence of a prosecutrix is not illegal on that ground alone. However, a judgment must indicate that the judge was mindful of the rule of practice that seeks corroboration. If a judge finds corroboration is not needed, reasons must be given for dispensing with it. When corroboration is necessary, it must come from an independent source, through direct or circumstantial evidence, but it is not necessary that it confirms every detail of the victim's testimony.
obiter: In the case of a grown up and married woman, it is always safe to insist on such corroboration.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: A reading of the deposition of the complainant shows that it has a ring of truth around it. The trial court has in the case before us found that the evidence of the complainant had been corroborated in material particulars by the evidence of Sheikh Lafid (P.W. I), Juman Nadaf (P.W. 2) and Jitrai (P.W. 4) the husband of the complainant. The High Court also has acted on the evidence of these witnesses.
legal_tests_applied: If a conviction is based on the evidence of a prosecutrix without any corroboration it will not be illegal on that sole ground. In the case of a grown up and married woman it is always safe to insist on such corroboration.

Wherever corroboration is necessary it should be from an independent source but it is not necessary that every part of the evidence of the victim should be confirmed in very detail by independent evidence. Such corroboration can be sought from either direct evidence or circumstantial evidence or from both.
The statement made by the complainant to her husband immediately after the incident is admissible under section 157 of the Indian Evidence Act and has a corroborative value.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant's argument that the evidence was insufficient was rejected because the court found the complainant's deposition had a 'ring of truth' and was adequately corroborated by other witnesses, whose testimony the trial court and High Court found no good ground to discard.
why_respondent_won: The complainant's deposition was found to have a 'ring of truth around it'.
The complainant's evidence was corroborated in material particulars by Sheikh Lafid (P.W. 1), who stated that he saw the appellant on the body of the complainant.
The evidence was also corroborated by Juman Nadaf (P.W. 2), who stated that when he heard the complainant's cry, he saw the appellant fleeing from the place.

The complainant's husband, Jitrai (P.W. 4), provided corroborating testimony that the complainant had told him the details of the incident shortly after it took place, which is admissible under Section 157 of the Indian Evidence Act.
policy_considerations: There must be an indication in the course of the judgment that the judge had this rule [of seeking corroboration] in his mind when he prepared the judgment and if in a given case the judge finds that there is no need for such corroboration he should give reasons for dispensing with the necessity for such corroboration.
